q: Who is the author of the lesson "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: Shivpoojan Sahay
Kamleshwar
Madhu Kankaria
Ajneya
e: The author of "Mata ka Anchal" is the renowned regional writer Shivpoojan Sahay.

q: What was Bholanath’s real name in the lesson "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: Shivnath
Kedarnath
Amarnath
Tarakeswarnath
e: The narrator’s real name was Tarakeswarnath, though his father affectionately called him Bholanath.

q: "Mata ka Anchal" is an excerpt from which novel by Shivpoojan Sahay?
o: Maila Anchal
Kitne Pakistan
Dehati Duniya
Godan
e: "Mata ka Anchal" is taken from Shivpoojan Sahay’s famous regional novel "Dehati Duniya" (1926).

q: What did Bholanath’s father apply on his forehead (lilar)?
o: Vermilion dot
Tripund of sacred ash (bhabhoot)
Tilak of roli
Turmeric paste
e: After worship, Babuji used to draw a tripund with sacred ash (bhabhoot) on Bholanath’s broad forehead.

q: What did Bholanath look like after applying sacred ash (bhabhoot)?
o: Bam Bhola
Kanhaiya
Hanuman
Ramchandra
e: With long matted hair and sacred ash smeared on his forehead, Bholanath looked just like "Bam Bhola".

q: What is the meaning of the word "Lilar" in the chapter?
o: Cheek
Chin
Neck
Forehead
e: "Lilar" is a regional Hindi word that means forehead.

q: What kind of hair did Bholanath have on his head?
o: Completely shaved head
White hair
Long matted locks
Short curly hair
e: The chapter mentions that in childhood Bholanath had long matted locks of hair on his head.

q: Where did Bholanath’s mother apply kohl (kajal)?
o: On his cheeks and ears
On his navel and forehead
Only in his eyes
On his palms and feet
e: To ward off the evil eye, Bholanath’s mother applied a dot of kohl on his navel and forehead.

q: What did the mother tie onto Bholanath’s braided hair?
o: A flowery tassel (lattoo)
A silk ribbon
A white thread
A silver bell
e: His mother braided his hair, tied a flowery tassel to it, and dressed him in a colorful kurta and cap like Kanhaiya.

q: Dressed up by his mother, what did Bholanath resemble as he came out sobbing?
o: A little monk
A prince
A wrestler
A veritable Kanhaiya
e: Wearing a colorful kurta and cap, Bholanath came out sobbing in Babuji’s lap looking just like Kanhaiya.

q: Which oil did Bholanath’s mother massage onto his head in childhood?
o: Jasmine oil
Almond oil
Mustard oil (karua tel)
Coconut oil
e: Bholanath’s mother soaked and massaged his head thoroughly with mustard oil (karua tel).

q: How many times did Bholanath’s father write Rama’s name in the Ramnama notebook?
o: Ten thousand times
One thousand times
Five hundred times
One hundred times
e: Every day during worship, Babuji used to write Rama’s name a thousand times in his "Ramnama bahi".

q: In how many flour balls did Babuji wrap the paper slips of Rama’s name to feed the fish in the Ganga?
o: Five hundred flour balls
One hundred flour balls
One thousand flour balls
Two hundred flour balls
e: Babuji wrote Rama’s name five hundred times on small paper slips, wrapped them in dough balls, and fed them to fish in the Ganga.

q: What kind of kiss did Babuji playfully ask Bholanath for?
o: Only a sweet kiss
Salty kiss
Forehead kiss
Sour and sweet kisses
e: Babuji would turn his right and left cheeks toward Bholanath and playfully ask for "sour and sweet" kisses.

q: What did Bholanath’s father feed him during his childhood?
o: Roti and greens
Halwa and gram
Curd and rice (goras-bhaat)
Puri and kheer
e: Babuji mixed curd and rice (goras-bhaat) in a brass bowl and fed it to Bholanath.

q: In whose names did the mother make morsels of food to feed Bholanath?
o: Gods and goddesses
Birds like parrot, myna, pigeon, swan, peacock
Kings and queens
Village friends
e: His mother made morsels in the names of birds—parrot, myna, pigeon, swan, and peacock—to persuade him to eat.

q: In childhood, what did Bholanath and his friends use to make jalebis in their pretend sweet shop?
o: Wet mud/clay
Wheat flour
Paper
Sand and grass
e: The children made jalebis from wet clay, laddoos from earthen lumps, puris from leaves, and batashe from broken pot shards.

q: In the children’s wedding procession game, what was used as the palanquin (palki)?
o: A wooden box
A brass plate
A bamboo basket
A broken mousetrap
e: In the wedding procession game, a broken mousetrap served as the palanquin and a mango sapling was rubbed as a shehnai.

q: What did the children use as a shehnai in their wedding procession game?
o: A paper horn
A brass whistle
By rubbing a sprouted mango plant (amaula)
A bamboo pipe
e: A tin canister served as a tambura and a sprouted mango sapling (amaula) was rubbed to play the shehnai.

q: In the song "Rahri mein rahri puran rahri...", what does the word "rahri" mean?
o: Earthen pot
Pigeon pea (arhar dal)
Paved road
Bullock cart
e: In the regional dialect, "rahri" refers to pigeon pea lentil (arhar dal).

q: Which fair (mela) is mentioned in the chapter "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: Dadri Fair
Sonpur Fair
Jagannathpur Fair
Dussehra Fair
e: The chapter mentions the Dadri Fair (Dadri ka mela) in the context of village life and boys’ rhymes.

q: Whom did Baiju tease by chanting "Budhwa beimaan maange karaila ka chokha"?
o: An old bridegroom
The school teacher
The village watchman
Moosan Tiwari
e: Moosan Tiwari had poor eyesight; Baiju teased him with this rhyme and the other boys joined in.

q: On Moosan Tiwari’s complaint, who went to Bholanath’s house to catch him?
o: Moosan Tiwari’s relatives
The village headman’s men
Four boys from the school
Village police constables
e: The school teacher sent four boys to catch Baiju and Bholanath; Bholanath was caught and later rescued by Babuji.

q: Whose burrow did the children start pouring water into?
o: A scorpion’s burrow
A mouse’s burrow
A rabbit’s burrow
A mongoose’s burrow
e: The narrator and his friends went to a mound and poured water into a mouse’s burrow to force it out.

q: What came out of the mouse’s burrow when the children poured water into it?
o: A snake
A big rat
A mongoose
A frog
e: When water was poured into the mouse’s burrow, a snake suddenly emerged, terrifying the children.

q: Fleeing in terror from the snake, where did Bholanath finally take shelter?
o: In Babuji’s lap
In the school
In a friend’s house
In his mother’s lap/anchal
e: Despite Babuji calling him, Bholanath did not stop and ran straight to hide in his mother’s anchal.

q: What did the narrator’s mother grind and apply to Bholanath’s wounds?
o: Tulsi
Sandalwood
Turmeric (haldi)
Neem leaves
e: His mother quickly ground turmeric, applied it to his thorn-scratched wounds, and comforted him.

q: What did the narrator find in the shelter of his mother’s anchal?
o: School textbooks
The shade of a canopy of love and peace
Only food and toys
Scolding and reprimand
e: At the end of the lesson, the narrator says he did not leave the shade of his mother’s anchal—the canopy of love and peace.

q: In which literary form/style is "Mata ka Anchal" written?
o: Autobiographical style
Epistolary (letter) style
Dramatic dialogue style
Reportage style
e: The chapter is written in an autobiographical first-person style depicting vivid childhood memories.

q: Which literary rasa predominates in the chapter "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: Veer Rasa (heroism)
Raudra Rasa (fury)
Bhayanak Rasa (terror)
Vatsalya Rasa (parental affection)
e: Because the entire chapter portrays boundless parental affection and childhood play, Vatsalya Rasa is predominant.

q: Why did Babuji deliberately grow slack and lose while wrestling with Bholanath?
o: Out of fear of the mother
Because Bholanath was physically stronger
To encourage little Bholanath and make him happy
Due to weakness and old age
e: Babuji intentionally lay flat on his back to delight Bholanath and boost his confidence.

q: What did Babuji do when Bholanath began pulling his moustache?
o: Pretended to cry and went to sleep
Laughingly kissed his hands and gently freed his moustache
Got angry and sent him out of the room
Complained to his mother
e: Instead of getting angry, Babuji laughed and affectionately kissed Bholanath’s little hands.

q: What complaint did Bholanath’s mother make to Babuji during mealtime?
o: That he fed tiny four-grain morsels which did not fill the child’s stomach
That he did not bathe the child on time
That he did not send the child to school
That he scolded the child too much
e: The mother complained that Babuji gave tiny four-grain morsels, saying a child cannot eat properly that way.

q: "Jab khayega bade-bade kaur, tab payega duniya mein thaur"—who said this?
o: Bholanath’s father (Babuji)
Moosan Tiwari
Baiju
Bholanath’s mother (Maiya)
e: Bholanath’s mother said this, believing that eating hearty, big morsels makes a child strong enough to find a place in the world.

q: Where did Bholanath’s father take him sitting on his shoulder?
o: To drop him at school
To irrigate the fields
To the Ganga to feed flour balls to the fish
To the city market to buy toys
e: After morning prayers, Babuji carried Bholanath on his shoulder to the Ganga to feed dough balls to the fish.

q: While returning from the Ganga, on the branch of which tree did Babuji swing Bholanath?
o: A thorny babool tree
Low-hanging branches of trees
Only a tall Peepal tree
A date palm tree
e: On the way back, Babuji would seat Bholanath on low-hanging branches of trees and swing him.

q: During the children’s play of farming, what served as the well’s pulley (ghirni) and bucket?
o: A makeshift pulley (garari) and an earthen potsherd (chukia)
An iron chain and bucket
A brass pot and silk rope
A glass bottle
e: At one end of the platform, the children set up a pretend well using twisted grass rope, a pulley, and a small earthen pot.

q: With what materials did the children make their playhouse and feast in "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: Plastic toys
Colored paper and cardboard
Wooden tables and chairs
Dust, sand, leaves, earthen lamps, and pebbles
e: The village children created an entire world of feasts and houses using dust, straw, leaves, earthen lamps, and mud lumps.

q: What did the children do when Babuji came and sat down in their pretend feast line (pangat)?
o: They sat silently out of fear
They asked him for money
They laughed, scattered the game, and ran away
They served him real food
e: As soon as Babuji sat down in the children’s pretend feast line, the children burst out laughing and ran away.

q: Why did the old bridegroom chase the children far away throwing clods of earth?
o: Because they stole his sweets
Because the children sang a teasing song upon seeing his palanquin
Because the children blocked his procession’s road
Because they threw stones at his horse
e: Angry at the children’s teasing song upon seeing his palanquin, the old bridegroom chased them away with clods of earth.

q: After being caught for teasing Moosan Tiwari, who rescued Bholanath?
o: His father (Babuji) by pleading politely
His mother by showing a broom
Baiju by fighting
The village landlord
e: When four boys caught Bholanath to take him to school, Babuji went and pleaded with the teacher and Tiwari to get him released.

q: What did the children do when a dust storm arrived in the mango orchard?
o: Hid under beds inside their homes
Climbed down into a well
Quietly returned to school
Ran toward the orchard to pick fallen mangoes and sang storm rhymes
e: As soon as the storm arrived, the children ran toward the orchard chanting rhymes to pick up fallen mangoes.

q: What did the children do when rain stopped and sunshine appeared during the rainy season?
o: Sailed boats in the pond
Baked clay pots
Came out from under trees and chased birds in the maize fields
Opened their books to study
e: After the rain subsided, the children ran into the maize fields trying to chase and catch birds.

q: During the heavy downpour, under which did the children huddle together?
o: In a cattle shed
Pressed close against the root of a tree
On a temple veranda
Under the school roof
e: To shelter from the sudden storm and heavy downpour, the children huddled tightly against a tree root.

q: Failing to catch birds in the maize field, what game did the children start on the mound?
o: Pouring water into a mouse’s burrow
Flying kites
Playing kabaddi
Playing gilli-danda
e: When they failed to catch birds, the boys moved to a mound and began pouring water into a mouse’s burrow.

q: What happened to Bholanath’s body as he ran away in panic from the snake?
o: He suffered no injury at all
He climbed up a tree
He reached home laughing
His body got scratched by thorns and the soles of his feet bled
e: Running blindly in terror, Bholanath fell repeatedly; his head was bruised and his soles were torn and bleeding from thorns.

q: Where was Babuji sitting when the injured Bholanath reached home?
o: Praying in the temple
Working in the fields
Sitting in the veranda (osara) smoking a hookah
Eating in the kitchen
e: Babuji was sitting in the veranda smoking his hookah and rushed forward upon hearing Bholanath’s cries.

q: What did Bholanath do when Babuji tried to take him from his mother’s lap into his own?
o: Showed his wounds to Babuji and laughed
Clung even tighter to his mother’s anchal and refused to leave its shade
Immediately climbed onto Babuji’s shoulder
Ran outside angry at his mother
e: In extreme fear and pain, Bholanath felt safest in his mother’s anchal and refused to leave her embrace.

q: What did Bholanath’s father do every morning after bathing and completing his prayers?
o: Seated Bholanath beside him, applied ash-tilak, and showed him the mirror
Left immediately for city office work
Slept throughout the day
Ploughed the fields
e: After worship, Babuji applied sacred ash on Bholanath’s forehead and showed him his reflection in a mirror.

q: How did Bholanath react when Babuji showed him his reflection in the mirror?
o: Broke the mirror
Started crying in fear
Made faces and ran away
Smiled shyly at first and then gently put the mirror down
e: When Babuji asked how he looked, Bholanath would smile bashfully and put the mirror down.

q: Who gave Tarakeswarnath the nickname "Bholanath"?
o: His elder brother
His school teacher
His father (Babuji) out of affection
The village priest
e: Although his formal name was Tarakeswarnath, his father affectionately nicknamed him Bholanath.

q: What does the narrator say at the beginning of the chapter about his relationship with his father and mother?
o: He slept only with his grandmother
He stayed mostly with his father and had only a feeding bond with his mother initially
He stayed day and night only with his mother
He was deeply afraid of his father
e: The narrator notes that he spent almost all his time with his father, and early on had only a milk-feeding bond with his mother.

q: Where and with whom did Bholanath sleep at night in early childhood?
o: With Babuji in his sitting room (baithak)
Alone on the terrace
At a friend’s house
Near the kitchen
e: In childhood, Bholanath slept in the sitting room with Babuji, woke up with him, and ate with him.

q: How did the children enact buying and selling in their play sweet-shop?
o: Using real paper notes
By writing credit in a ledger
Using grains of wheat
Using potsherds as coins, and Babuji sometimes gave real Gorakhpuriya coins
e: The children used potsherd coins, and Babuji occasionally joined their game by buying sweets with Gorakhpuriya copper coins.

q: What was the greatest specialty of Bholanath’s childhood games?
o: Playing alone inside a closed room
Avoiding imitation of adults
Creating collective, imaginative games out of nature and everyday objects
Using expensive imported toys
e: The village children creatively built weddings, farming, and feasts using clay, leaves, broken pots, and tin cans.

q: What does the word "Amaula" signify in the chapter?
o: The name of a folk song
A small newly sprouted mango plant
A type of earthen pot
A monsoon mushroom
e: In regional parlance, a newly sprouted mango sapling is called an "amaula", which children rubbed to make a whistle/shehnai.

q: In what context does the proverb "Jahan ladkon ka sang tahan baje mridang..." appear in the chapter?
o: When Bholanath joined his peer group of boys and burst into lively play
When a fair took place in the village
When Babuji went to school
When a wedding happened at home
e: As soon as Bholanath saw his group of friends, he forgot his tears, hopped off Babuji’s lap, and plunged into lively play.

q: Which sacred text did Babuji read regularly every day?
o: Rigveda
Manusmriti
Padmavat
Ramayana
e: After morning rituals, Babuji regularly recited the Ramayana while Bholanath sat beside him.

q: What does "Osara" mean in the chapter?
o: A corner of the kitchen
The village crossroads
The veranda or porch outside the house
The ridge of a field
e: In rural homes, the front porch or veranda is called "osara", where Babuji was smoking his hookah.

q: In the farming game, what rural activities did the children imitate?
o: Taking a school examination
Ploughing, irrigating with a water lift, sowing seeds, and weighing the harvest
Selling grain in a city market
Cooking food and washing clothes
e: Observing village life, the children vividly enacted ploughing, irrigation, harvesting, and weighing crops in play.

q: Passage: "Babuji bathed us and seated us for worship. We would pester him to apply the sacred ash tilak." — What trait of the child is revealed here?
o: Childlike insistence and innocent fondness toward his father
Deep fear of religious rituals
Anger and rebellion toward his father
A sense of vanity
e: Bholanath pestering his father for the ash tilak highlights innocent childhood stubbornness and paternal closeness.

q: Passage: "Sometimes Babuji wrestled with us. Growing slack, he boosted our strength and we pinned him down." — What is the psychological purpose of this behavior?
o: To train the child as a professional wrestler
To lie down due to personal fatigue
To frighten the child by feigning weakness
To instill confidence, enthusiasm, and a joyful sense of triumph in the child
e: A sensitive parent lets the child win in play to nurture self-confidence and emotional bonding.

q: Passage: "When he eats big morsels, only then will he find his place in the world." — What contrast does this show between the mother’s and father’s way of feeding?
o: The mother feeds only sweets and the father only fruits
Both force-feed the child harshly
The father is easily satisfied in affection, whereas the mother practically worries about full nourishment
The father wants to starve the child while the mother gets angry
e: The father’s care shows gentle indulgence, while the mother combines tenderness with practical concern for nutrition.

q: Passage: "Our crying lasted only until we spotted our band of friends while in Babuji’s lap." — What truth of child psychology does this establish?
o: Children cry only to go outdoors
A child’s sorrow is momentary and instantly dissolves in the joy of peers and play
The child dislikes his parents
Children always fake their tears
e: A child’s mind lives in the moment; seeing friends immediately erases the distress of oil massage and braiding.

q: Passage: "Shortly after closing down (badhakar) the sweet shop, we built a playhouse." — What does the idiom "dukaan badhana" mean here?
o: To close down or wind up the shop
To expand the size of the shop
To add new sweets to the shop
To move the shop outside the village
e: In traditional Hindi usage, "dukaan badhana" is an auspicious idiom meaning to close or wind up a shop.

q: Passage: "If a wedding procession passed, the children played a tin tambura and mango-sapling shehnai." — What social tendency does this reflect?
o: Children opposed the institution of marriage
Music was the only topic children knew
Playing real shehnai was banned in the village
Children observe surrounding social customs and creatively imitate them in play
e: Children’s play mirrors their social environment; observing village weddings inspired them to recreate processions in play.

q: Passage: "Seeing Moosan Tiwari from afar, Baiju teased—‘Budhwa beimaan maange karaila ka chokha’." — What tendency of children is reflected here?
o: Organized violence against elders
Seriousness toward academics
Mischievous impulse to tease elders playfully and run away without deep malice
A plot to seize someone’s property
e: Driven by carefree mischief, children tease elders thoughtlessly without ill intent and panic when caught.

q: When Babuji rescued Bholanath from school, what happened on the way back when he saw his playmates?
o: Babuji locked him inside a room
He met Baiju and friends, forgot his fear, and ran off to play with them again
He quietly went home and studied
He got Baiju arrested
e: As soon as the danger passed and he saw his friends, Bholanath forgot the scolding and rejoined their play.

q: Passage: "A storm came, the sky filled with dark clouds, and clusters of trees began to roar." — How is nature depicted here?
o: As a vivid, dynamic, and thrilling depiction of sudden rural weather change
As suffering from urban pollution
As an arid desert climate
As heavy mountain snowfall
e: Shivpoojan Sahay paints a highly natural, vivid sensory picture of a sudden monsoon storm and downpour.

q: Passage: "Babuji rushed to take me from Maiya’s lap into his own, yet I did not leave the shade of Maiya’s anchal." — Which central theme does this prove?
o: Fathers do not love their children
The child never goes out with his father
The mother stays home only during crises
A father may be a companion in joy and play, but in extreme terror and pain a child finds ultimate refuge in the mother’s anchal
e: This is the core message and title justification: in moments of crisis, the child instinctively seeks peace and safety in his mother’s anchal.

q: If a modern urban child were in Bholanath’s place, what would be the main difference in play compared to "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: Urban children never love their parents
Urban children only attend the Dadri fair
Instead of collective outdoor play with mud and leaves, indoor electronic or solitary games would dominate
Urban children only pour water in mouse burrows
e: The rural childhood in the story thrives in nature and community, unlike modern urban childhood dominated by screens and indoor life.

q: Which Indian cultural belief is reflected when the mother oils Bholanath, applies kohl, and dresses him like Kanhaiya?
o: Following a rigid ritual rule
Protecting the child from the evil eye and seeing child Krishna’s image in him
Preparing the child to join a drama troupe
Showing off wealth to neighbors
e: Applying kohl dots protects against the evil eye, while dressing a son as baby Krishna (Kanhaiya) reflects traditional maternal affection.

q: What value of Babuji’s life is revealed by his writing Rama’s name and wrapping it in flour balls for the fish?
o: Devotion to God combined with compassion and kindness toward living creatures
Polluting the water out of superstition
Business of catching and selling fish
A habit of wasting time
e: Feeding dough balls to fish blends spiritual devotion with compassion and care for living beings.

q: Context: Water poured into a mouse burrow unexpectedly brings out a snake, just as if Shiva’s snake emerged to protect Ganesha’s mouse. What literary device is seen in this comparison?
o: Harsh political satire
Purely scientific explanation
Romantic description
Humorous and ironic expression through mythological allusion
e: Since the mouse is Ganesha’s mount and the snake adorns Shiva, the author playfully invokes myth to heighten the surprise.

q: What effect does the use of regional words like "goras-bhaat", "thekri", "lilar", and "osara" have on the narrative?
o: It makes the meaning completely unclear
It sounds like a foreign language
It brings vividness, intimacy, and authentic regional flavor (anchalikta) to the rural setting
It makes the language dull and difficult
e: Natural regional vocabulary immerses the reader directly into the rural Bihar setting of the early 20th century.

q: If a child is only lectured and never played with, what lesson does Babuji’s example in "Mata ka Anchal" offer?
o: Only teachers should interact with children
Parents should come down to the child’s level, play with them, and act as friends
Children should always be kept under strict discipline only
Parents should never talk to children
e: By joining feasts, losing wrestling matches, and swinging Bholanath, Babuji shows that joyful participation builds deep trust.

q: Which incident in the chapter reflects the proverb that carefree boys often do not realize the trouble they cause others ("ladke parayi peer nahi jaante")?
o: Teasing visually impaired Moosan Tiwari and the old groom, and chasing birds
Feeding flour balls to fish in the Ganga
Hiding in the mother’s lap while crying
Listening to the Ramayana with Babuji
e: In playful excitement, the boys do not realize how much their teasing hurts or angers Moosan Tiwari or the old groom.

q: At the end of "Mata ka Anchal", Bholanath’s refusal to go to Babuji was not out of dislike—what was the real reason?
o: Bholanath feared Babuji would send him to school
Babuji had beaten Bholanath earlier
Mother had forbidden him from talking to Babuji
In moments of intense terror and pain, a child instinctively seeks safety in the mother’s tender anchal
e: Even though he spent his whole day with Babuji, in a moment of sheer terror Bholanath instinctively trusted his mother’s lap most.

q: What does the inclusion of folk rhymes like "Ek paisa ki laai, bazaar mein chhitrai..." show in the chapter?
o: An economic survey of market inflation
A mandatory syllabus lesson
The oral folk tradition and spontaneous joy of rural children of that era
A strict classical poetry examination
e: Children’s folk rhymes bring out the spontaneous rhythm, collective joy, and oral culture of rural childhood.

q: When the injured child ran home crying, how did Babuji respond instead of getting angry at his mischief?
o: He sent Bholanath back to the mound
He immediately dropped the hookah, rushed forward, and tried to comfort the child in his lap
He beat Bholanath with a stick
He shut the door
e: Without scolding or questioning, Babuji immediately rushed anxiously upon hearing the cry to hold his child.

q: Passage: "Mother quickly hid me in her anchal and began asking about my condition while weeping." — What trait of the mother emerges here?
o: Deeply sensitive, compassionate motherhood that feels the child’s pain as her own
Negligence toward the child
Concern only for household chores
Habit of blaming the father
e: Seeing her child hurt makes the mother weep too, reflecting the boundless empathy of a mother’s heart.

q: What kind of family environment do the actions of Bholanath’s father and mother create?
o: A harsh, fearful, and lonely environment
A greedy and fiercely competitive environment
An environment of ridicule and neglect
A balanced environment filled with affection, security, cultural values, and free childhood growth
e: The father nurtures play and social warmth while the mother provides nourishment and refuge, creating a wholesome family.

q: In the children’s wedding game in "Mata ka Anchal", how was the wedding procession staged?
o: They rented real elephants and horses
They only drew pictures
Children acted as samdhi and groom, parading through the courtyard with improvised props
They invited the real village priest
e: The children marched their procession across the porch, improvising roles of groom, samdhi, and wedding rituals.

q: What is the context of Babuji giving "Gorakhpuriya coins" to Bholanath?
o: To pay a fine to Moosan Tiwari
When the children set up their pretend sweet shop, Babuji joined in by buying items with real copper coins
To pay school fees
To buy tickets at the fair
e: Participating cheerfully in their game, Babuji handed over copper coins to buy their clay sweets, delighting the children.

q: In the farming game, how did the children prepare the "soil" and simulate the harvest?
o: They planted twigs/leaves among pebbles, irrigated them, and weighed dust/leaves as harvested grain
They harvested real wheat crops
They brought boats from the river
They painted stones
e: Treating the platform as a field, they planted twigs, watered them from their pretend well, and mimed harvesting and weighing.

q: Why did Bholanath resist when his mother oiled and braided his hair?
o: Because he was allergic to oil
Because his friends mocked him

q: Although the father’s presence dominates the earlier part of the excerpt, why did the author still title it "Mata ka Anchal"?

Because the mother was the school principal
e: The narrative arc culminates in the psychological truth that in terror, even a father’s fondness cannot replace a mother’s protective anchal.

q: Which conclusion is most accurate when comparing childhood in "Mata ka Anchal" with childhood today?
o: Earlier childhood was rooted in nature, community, and spontaneous creativity, whereas today’s is more solitary and screen-dependent
Children earlier received no time from parents
Children today play more mud games
Children earlier lacked imagination
e: A central NCERT/JAC reflection point is that despite fewer material goods, childhood back then was richer in social bonding and creativity.

q: How does Babuji’s character blend "tradition" with "child-friendly companionship"?
o: He only prays and keeps the child away

He only forces rote memorization of grammar

e: Babuji’s character demonstrates that spiritual discipline and warm, playful parenting can coexist harmoniously.

q: What aspect of contemporary society do the "platform drama" and "harvest-weighing game" highlight?
o: Maritime trade and shipping traditions
Functioning of urban stock markets
The deep imprint of an agrarian rural economy and folk culture on children’s minds
Life of workers in industrial factories
e: Children enact what they see around them; wells, irrigation, and crop weighing reflect their agrarian village world.

q: What psychological aspect is revealed by the boys teasing Moosan Tiwari and then panicking when caught?
o: Babuji had provoked them to do it
In a group, children feel bold and mischievous, but when confronted with consequences, their innocent fear surfaces
The children were skilled in organized crime
The teacher was jealous of the children
e: Peer-group boldness drives thoughtless pranks, while individual confrontation immediately reveals their vulnerable childhood fear.

q: Where does dramatic contrast appear most powerfully in "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: Constant companionship with the father throughout the day versus seeking sole refuge in the mother’s anchal during crisis
Between summer and winter
Between village and foreign lands
Between king and pauper
e: This contrast gives the story emotional depth: the boy who lives beside his father all day turns exclusively to his mother in fear.

q: If all regional words (lilar, rahri, goras, thekri, osara) were replaced with formal standard Hindi, how would it affect the text?
o: The text would become more rural and engaging
Vatsalya rasa would multiply
The plot would turn historical
The earthy authenticity, rural fragrance, and cultural liveliness of the text would be diminished
e: Regional diction is the soul of this narrative, grounding the reader in the authentic rural milieu.

q: On what basis is "Dehati Duniya" (from which "Mata ka Anchal" is taken) regarded as Hindi’s earliest regional novel?
o: Because it contains only royal court events
Because it is written in verse
Because it centers on the dialect, folk songs, customs, and daily life of a specific rural region
Because it is based on European villages
e: Published in 1926, "Dehati Duniya" pioneered making a specific region’s dialect, folklore, and rural life central to the novel.

q: What literary skill is reflected in the phrase "the shade of the canopy of love and peace" (prem aur shanti ke chandove ki chhaya)?
o: Describing anger and revenge
Using metaphor to give tangible form to maternal affection as a protective canopy
Explaining tent-construction techniques
Confusing the reader with exaggeration
e: Calling the anchal a "canopy of love and peace" is a poignant metaphor portraying maternal shelter as cooling and fearless.

q: Where in the children’s play or observations does a subtle glimpse of rural social realities/customs appear?

Feeding flour balls to fish
Sheltering under a tree in rain
Braiding hair
e: The old bridegroom in the procession subtly reflects the contemporary social reality of mismatched marriages.

q: Why does the narrator frequently use the first-person plural pronoun "हम" (we) while narrating his childhood?
o: Because the narrator had five twin siblings
To follow English grammar rules
To make the text look like an official report
To reflect the natural Bhojpuri/Bihar colloquial idiom and convey a shared, collective childhood
e: In eastern Hindi/Bihar speech, using "hum" for "I" is natural, and it also captures the collective spirit of childhood.

q: In what role is "nature" present in the children’s lives in "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: As a difficult school subject
As an absent backdrop
As a living playground and source of toys, rather than mere background decoration
Only as a dangerous enemy
e: Clay, storms, rain, mango saplings, maize fields, and tree branches are integral companions in the children’s play.

q: Babuji calmly rescuing Bholanath from school without harsh beating exemplifies which principle of parenting?
o: Depriving the child of education
Supporting and guiding a child calmly in trouble rather than humiliating them
Ignoring every mischief permanently
Rejecting the teacher’s authority completely
e: Babuji handles the situation with grace, pacifying the elders and protecting his child without humiliation.

q: Which incidents in the chapter best prove that "children do not hold onto tears, pain, or quarrels for long"?

Hiding in his mother’s anchal after seeing the snake
Babuji writing in his Ramnama notebook
Mother grinding turmeric
e: Both incidents show how swiftly a child’s tears or fear vanish when play and companions beckon.

q: What kind of structural turning point does the emergence of the snake bring to the narrative?
o: It turns the story into a detective mystery
It introduces a science lesson
It marks the father’s first appearance
It shifts the narrative abruptly from carefree humor and play to terror, pathos, and the touching climax in the mother’s anchal
e: The snake episode transforms the lighthearted flow of games into a deeply moving emotional climax of maternal refuge.

They make the narrative sluggish
e: These folk rhymes add rhythm and sound imagery, making the children’s joyful commotion come alive.

q: Which social stereotype is broken by the portrayal of Babuji in "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: The idea that mothers cook food
The stereotype that a father must remain stern, aloof, and uninvolved in nurturing a young child
The idea that villagers are not religious
The idea that children play outside
e: Babuji bathes, feeds, swings, and plays with his son, presenting a deeply tender and involved model of fatherhood.

q: What is the symbolic difference between the mother dressing him as "Kanhaiya" and the father shaping him as "Bam Bhola"?
o: The father adorns him simply with ash like Shiva, whereas the mother decks him with kohl, braid, and colorful clothes like charming Krishna
They are rivals to each other
Father wanted him to be a soldier and mother a monk
Neither form relates to the story
e: The father’s simple ash-tilak (Bhola) and the mother’s tender adornment (Kanhaiya) capture two complementary facets of Indian domestic love.

q: Despite being autobiographical, why does "Mata ka Anchal" feel universal rather than the story of just one individual?
o: Because no character is named in it
Because it is futuristic science fiction
Because it avoids all emotions
Because childhood innocence, imaginative play, fear, and instinctive bond with a mother are universal human experiences
e: Bholanath’s childhood awakens memories of every reader’s own early years and maternal warmth, making it timeless and universal.

q: What is the figurative meaning of the mother’s link between "eating big morsels" and "finding a place in the world"?
o: One must buy land to live in the world
Light eaters are exiled from society
A healthy, well-nourished body provides the strength to stand firm and thrive in life’s struggles
Only heavy eaters become wealthy
e: In the mother’s practical wisdom, physical nourishment is the foundation for resilience and success in life.

q: Why is Shivpoojan Sahay’s narrative style described as "pictorial" (chitratmak)?
o: Because he ends the story in two sentences
Because through vivid minute details (ash, kohl, potsherds, storm, burrow), he brings entire scenes alive before the reader’s eyes
Because the book contains only pictures and no words
Because he was an art teacher
e: His sharp sensory details make every scene unfold like a vivid motion picture in the reader’s imagination.

q: What role does the contrast between "Baiju" (the initiator) and "Bholanath" (the follower caught) play in the story?
o: It shows Bholanath is innocent and easily swept up by peers rather than being the mastermind
It proves Baiju never went to school
It shows Bholanath was extremely cunning
It has no relevance to the story
e: Baiju initiates the prank and escapes swiftly while simple Bholanath gets caught, fitting his very nickname.

q: Which of the following is the best example of gentle humor in "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: Running bleeding from the snake
Mother weeping while applying turmeric
Being chased by four schoolboys
Babuji asking for sour-sweet kisses, losing wrestling, and sitting in the children’s pretend feast
e: Gentle, heartwarming humor shines through Babuji’s playful interactions and the children’s mock adult rituals.

q: The mother grinding turmeric for wounds and the father making flour balls for fish together reflect which Indian way of life?
o: Modern hospital infrastructure
Royal luxury
Nature-aligned, self-reliant, and compassionate traditional household living
Mechanical consumerist living
e: Everyday actions weave together home remedies, compassion for animals, and unpretentious family harmony.

q: Considering the love of both parents in "Mata ka Anchal", why can the story not be seen as denying paternal love?
o: Because the child ends up in the father’s lap
Because paternal affection fills most of the narrative; the ending simply highlights the unique refuge of a mother in crisis
Because the mother never appears
Because the father wrote the lesson
e: Both parents’ love is deeply honored; the finale distinguishes their complementary roles rather than diminishing the father’s devotion.

q: Which aspect of play in "Mata ka Anchal" reinforces that "children’s games are free from social discrimination"?
o: All neighborhood boys sit together in the feast line, act out wedding roles, and share games freely
Children play only alone at home
They allow only rich kids to join
They select friends by status
e: The group of playmates unites effortlessly across all games of feasting, farming, and drama without barriers.

q: What broader reality can the "snake" symbolize in the arc of childhood depicted in "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: Religious ignorance
Destruction of crops
School examinations
Unexpected terror or crisis in life that abruptly shatters the carefree world of play
e: Emerging amidst carefree play, the snake represents sudden life crisis that drives the child back to maternal security.

q: Which statement best encapsulates the core sensibility of "Mata ka Anchal"?
o: Only academics should matter in childhood
Rural life is wholly backward and miserable
Innocent childhood play, a father’s tender companionship, and a mother’s fearless shelter in crisis are life’s priceless treasures
Childhood is incomplete without wealth and status
e: This triad—innocent play, paternal warmth, and maternal refuge—forms the emotional soul of the entire chapter.

q: In a JAC exam question, what stylistic feature do concrete details like "kohl, sacred ash, and leaf-puris" demonstrate?
o: Blind imitation of foreign literature
Realistic regional imagery and keen observation of folk life
Abstract philosophical mysticism
Use of scientific terminology
e: These concrete, sensory details prove the author’s sharp observation of folk culture and realistic regional craft.
